Which song, featured in the 1934 film 'The Gay Divorcee,' won the very first Academy Award for Best Original Song?
questions.explanation: At the 7th Academy Awards ceremony in 1935, "The Continental" became the first-ever winner of the Best Original Song Oscar. The song was performed by Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire in the film, and it was so popular it even inspired a dance craze of the same name.

questions.question: Which actor won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his role in Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood?
questions.explanation: Brad Pitt took home the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor at the 2020 Academy Awards for his portrayal of stuntman Cliff Booth in Quentin Tarantino's Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. It was Pitt's first acting Oscar win, though he had previously won as a producer for 12 Years a Slave. His charming acceptance speech was widely praised as one of the highlights of the ceremony.

questions.question: Film critic Lotte Eisner coined what German term to describe the shadowy, twilight-like interior lighting style characteristic of German Expressionist cinema?
questions.explanation: Lotte Eisner, in her landmark study "The Haunted Screen," used the term "helldunkel" (meaning light-dark, akin to chiaroscuro) to describe the moody, shadow-drenched lighting of German Expressionist films. She saw it as a visual manifestation of a uniquely German romantic soul, rooted in the contrast between light and darkness. This aesthetic profoundly influenced later Hollywood film noir cinematography.

questions.question: American films from the 1960s that were made in the style of classic film noir — but are not classified as film noir proper — are recognized as an early precursor phase to what broader cinematic movement that fully emerged in the 1970s and beyond?
questions.explanation: Classic film noir is generally considered to span the 1940s and 1950s, but the 1960s produced a wave of American films — such as "Harper" (1966) and "Point Blank" (1967) — that borrowed its dark aesthetics and themes without being classified as noir proper. These films are now seen as an early precursor phase to neo-noir, the broader movement that reimagined and revived noir conventions from the 1970s onward. Neo-noir has since become a rich and enduring genre, encompassing works like "Chinatown" (1974) and "Blade Runner" (1982).
